questions.question: Let $F(x) = \int_a^x f(t)\,\mathrm{d}t$ with $f$ Riemann integrable on $[a,b]$. What does Part 1 of the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus always guarantee about $F$ on $[a,b]$?
options: $F$ is differentiable at every point of $[a,b]$.

questions.question: At an interior point $x_0\in(a,b)$, which extra assumption allows Part 1 of the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus to conclude that $F'(x_0) = f(x_0)$ for $F(x) = \int_a^x f(t)\,\mathrm{d}t$?
If $f(x) = x^2$ and $F(x) = \int_0^x t^2\,\mathrm{d}t$, what is $F'(x)$?
Let $F(x) = \int_2^x 5\,\mathrm{d}t$. What is $F'(x)$?
Which statement best captures the interpretation of Part 1 of the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus?
options: Integration and differentiation are unrelated because one uses areas and the other uses slopes.
Integration creates an accumulation function, and differentiation recovers the integrand at points of continuity.
Differentiation always produces a discontinuous function.
A Riemann integral can only be defined for differentiable functions.

questions.question: Suppose $f$ is Riemann integrable on $[a,b]$ but not known to be continuous at some interior point $x_0$. What can Part 1 still guarantee?
Use the variable-limits formula from the definition. If $H(x) = \int_x^{x^2} f(t)\,\mathrm{d}t$, which expression equals $H'(x)$?
Let $K(x) = \int_{x^3}^{2x} f(t)\,\mathrm{d}t$. What is $K'(x)$?
Why does the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus state the differentiability conclusion at $x_0\in(a,b)$ rather than at every point of $[a,b]$?
options: Because the integrand must be discontinuous at both endpoints
Because every integrable function is discontinuous at endpoints
Because endpoints require separate one-sided derivative statements
Because continuity forces the interval to collapse to one point

questions.question: Which prerequisite is most directly used when concluding from the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus that $F'(x_0) = f(x_0)$?
options: Continuity, because the theorem requires $f$ to be continuous at $x_0$.
Only Riemann integrability, because no local assumption is needed.
Only antiderivatives, because Part 1 is about evaluating definite integrals.
None of the prerequisites, because the conclusion is purely algebraic.

questions.question: Suppose $J(x) = \int_{\sin x}^{x^2+1} f(t)\,\mathrm{d}t$. What is $J'(x)$?
Let $F(x) = \int_a^x f(t)\,\mathrm{d}t$. If $f$ is continuous at an interior point $x_0$ and $f(x_0) = 7$, what does the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus give?
options: The value of $F$ itself is forced to be $7$ at $x_0$.

questions.question: What function is built from $f$ in Part 1 of the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus?
What does Riemann integrability of $f$ guarantee for $F(x)=\int_a^x f(t)\,\mathrm{d}t$?
At a point where $f$ is continuous, what does differentiating the accumulation function recover?
options: The length of the interval only.
The square of the upper limit only.

questions.question: If $F(x)=\int_0^x \cos t\,\mathrm{d}t$, what is $F'(x)$?
If $F(x)=\int_1^x t\,\mathrm{d}t$, what is $F'(x)$?
Using the variable-limit rule, what is $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}\int_0^{x^2} f(t)\,\mathrm{d}t$?
What can fail if $f$ is Riemann integrable but not continuous at an interior point $x_0$?
options: The continuity of $F$ on $[a,b]$ is lost automatically.
The integral defining $F$ cannot be written.
The lower limit must equal the upper limit.

questions.question: Let $H(x)=\int_x^{3x} t^2\,\mathrm{d}t$. What is $H'(x)$?
